In Lab 7, we will go back to the King County sales data from maintained by Andy Krause at Zillow. You can find the datasets and Readme file in this repository.

Lab 7 comes in two parts, released separately. This is Part A, where we use classical regression, which considers more on the model specification, assumptions, and parameter interpretation. We cover two models: linear regression for a continuous outcome (King County sale prices) and logistic regression for a binary outcome (mortgage denial in the Boston HMDA data). Part B (released after the machine learning lecture) still uses regression but under the context of machine learning, where we care about the prediction accuracy on unseen test dataset. A seminal paper discusses the two cultures in statistical modeling: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures. Leo Breiman. 2001.

From Lab 4, the use of any generative AI tool (ChatGPT, Copilot, etc.) is allowed for coding assignments. But, I still encourage you to write codes by yourself and use AI tools as a way to debug and explore new knowledge. More information about Academic Integrity and the Use of AI.

Lab 07 Regression in Statistics

# --- install packages (run once, then keep these lines commented out) ---
#install.packages("modelsummary") # formats regression tables
#install.packages("devtools")     # lets us install packages from GitHub (needed on Windows)
#devtools::install_github('andykrause/kingCoData') # the King County sales data package

# --- load packages (run every time you open R) ---
library('tidyverse')   # data wrangling (dplyr, tidyr) and plotting (ggplot2)
library(modelsummary)  # side by side regression result tables
## Warning: package 'modelsummary' was built under R version 4.6.2
library('kingCoData')  # King County home sales data
data(kingco_sales) # load the sale data
# only select the sales in 2023
sales <- kingco_sales %>% 
  filter(sale_date >= as.Date("2023-01-01") & sale_date <= as.Date("2023-12-31"))

A Simple Linear Regression

Checking Correlation

Correlation (r) measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables. The most common one for continuous numeric data is Pearson correlation, which ranges from -1 to 1.

  • +1 Perfect positive correlation
  • 0 No linear relationship
  • –1 Perfect negative correlation

Note: Correlation is a useful starting point for selecting variables. We often use |r|>0.3 as a rough criterion for inclusion. But we still need to incorporate domain knowledge and some diagnostic testing. For example, correlation between sale price and year built is only ~0.1, which suggests a weak linear relationship, but it may still be theoretically relevant.

# Pearson correlation matrix for four numeric variables
# each cell is the correlation (r) between the row and the column variable
cor(sales[, c("sale_price", "sqft", "year_built", "condition")])
##             sale_price        sqft   year_built   condition
## sale_price 1.000000000  0.53927682  0.005699814  0.01146259
## sqft       0.539276825  1.00000000  0.295748914 -0.06728411
## year_built 0.005699814  0.29574891  1.000000000 -0.36754450
## condition  0.011462589 -0.06728411 -0.367544504  1.00000000

Scatterplots

# reshape from wide to long: one row per (house, variable) pair
# this lets us draw both scatterplots with one ggplot call using facets
sales_long <- sales |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(sqft, year_built), # the two X variables we want to plot
    names_to = "variable",      # new column holding the variable name
    values_to = "xvalue"        # new column holding the X value
  )

ggplot(sales_long, aes(x = xvalue, y = sale_price)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.3, alpha = 0.5, color = "#e8e3d3") +   # one point per sale
  geom_smooth(linewidth = 0.5, method = "lm", formula = "y~x",
              color = "#4b2e83") +                          # straight OLS line
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +  # one panel per X, each with its own x axis
  labs(
    x = "Explanatory Variable",
    y = "Sale Price ($)",
    title = "Sale Price vs. Square Footage of House (Sqft) and Year Built"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Reading the plot: in the sqft panel, price rises with house size and the purple line slopes clearly upward. The cloud also fans out: small houses sell in a narrow price range, while large houses spread from about $1 million to over $10 million. That is an early sign of unequal variance. In the year_built panel, the line is almost flat, so age alone has a weak linear link with price (this matches r≈0.1). In both panels, a handful of sales sit far above the rest ($10 to $16.5 million). Keep them in mind; we will meet them again as outliers.

Fitting the Model

Starting to fit a regression, you define a family of models that express a precise, but generic, pattern that you want to capture. For example, the pattern might be a straight line, or a quadratic curve. You will express the model family as an equation like y=β0+β1x or y=β0+β1x2. Here, x and y are known variables from your data, and β0 and β1 are parameters that can vary to capture different patterns.

# lm() fits a linear model by ordinary least squares (OLS)
# formula: Y ~ X1 + X2; R adds the intercept for us
simple_lm <- lm(data = sales, sale_price ~ sqft + year_built)

We can check the results using summary() (result table) and confint() (confidence intervals).

summary(simple_lm) # coefficients, standard errors, t values, p values, R-squared
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = sale_price ~ sqft + year_built, data = sales)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -1845377  -321881   -93956   172424 13848369 
## 
## Coefficients:
##               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept) 8023953.22  325413.85   24.66   <2e-16 ***
## sqft            501.08       5.93   84.50   <2e-16 ***
## year_built    -4022.48     166.39  -24.17   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 645400 on 15406 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.3167, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3166 
## F-statistic:  3571 on 2 and 15406 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
confint(simple_lm) # 95% confidence interval for each coefficient
##                    2.5 %       97.5 %
## (Intercept) 7386103.6761 8661802.7661
## sqft            489.4558     512.7013
## year_built    -4348.6282   -3696.3264

How to read the tables?

Click to view additional notes on reading the results

Hypothesis: The model test if Y is associated with X. The null hypothesis H0 is that there is no linear relationship between the response variable and the explanatory variable(s), and the alternative hypothesis H1 is that there is relationship.

Estimate and standard error:In the model, estimate is the estimation of coefficient β, std.error is the standard error for estimation. The standard error of the coefficient is an estimate of the standard deviation of the coefficient β. In effect, it is telling us how much uncertainty there is with our coefficient. The standard error is often used to create confidence intervals.

t-statistic: The t-statistic is simply the coefficient divided by the standard error. In general, we want our coefficients to have large t-statistics, because it indicates that our standard error is small in comparison to our coefficient. Simply put, we are saying that the coefficient is t standard errors away from zero.

p-value: If you see the variable has p value ≤0.05, or you can also see the star next to Pr(>|t|)), we can say we reject the null hypothesis. In practice, any p-value below 0.05 is usually deemed as significant. What do we mean when we say significant? It means we are confident that the coefficient is not zero, meaning the coefficient does in fact add value to the model by helping to explain the variance within our dependent variable. Note: reading the stars this way only works for individual variables and not categorical variables.

R-squared: R-squared explains how much variation of y can be explained by the model. This is helpful for univariate regression, but starts to become fairly unhelpful for multivariate regression. We would look at adjusted R-squared, which penalizes complexity.

Check Assumptions

For a normal linear model to be a good model, there are some conditions/assumptions that need to be fulfilled. The six below match the “OLS Assumptions in Plain Words” table from lecture:

  1. Linearity: average Y changes along a straight line in X. Y can be described by a linear combination of X (or transformations of X). You may log or square X, but not β.
  2. Random sample, independent errors: each home is a fresh draw; one sale’s error tells us nothing about a neighbor’s. We are using time series and spatial data, so we are likely to violate this assumption.
  3. No perfect multicollinearity among X: no X is an exact copy or sum of other Xs. Example: using all three scores as X if total score = part A score + part B score.
  4. Zero conditional mean E[ε∣X]=0: nothing left in the error moves with X; no important variable is left out. If it fails, we get omitted-variable bias and the slope is wrong.
  5. Equal variance (homoscedasticity) Var(ε∣X)=σ2: errors spread the same way for cheap and expensive homes.
  6. Normal errors ε∼N(0,σ2): errors follow a bell curve.

How much each assumption buys you:

  • Assumptions 1–4 give unbiased slopes — right on average.
  • + Assumption 5 makes OLS BLUE — the most precise linear unbiased estimator (Gauss–Markov).
  • + Assumption 6 makes p-values exact even in a small sample, not just approximately.

If these assumptions are not met, the inference with the computed standard error is invalid. That is, if the assumptions are not met, the standard error should not be trusted, or should be computed using alternative methods.

The quickest way to check many assumptions is to use plot(model) and it will generated several key plots for us. We use which to specify the plot but in practice, you can generate them at the same time.

We will setup a ‘perfect’ model as the example to compare:

set.seed(519) # fix the random numbers so everyone gets the same "perfect" model

# simulate data that meets every OLS assumption:
# a true straight line (3 + 2x) plus normal noise with constant spread
example_x <- seq(1, 100, by = 1)
example_y <- 3 + 2 * example_x + rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 2)
example_model <- lm(example_y ~ example_x)

Residuals vs Fitted

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # put the next two plots side by side (1 row, 2 columns)

# which = 1 asks plot() for the Residuals vs Fitted panel only
plot(example_model, which = 1, main = "Perfect Model")
plot(simple_lm, which = 1, main = "Our Linear Model")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # reset to one plot per figure

Horizontal Axis: Fitted values (predicted values) from the regression model.

Vertical Axis: Residuals (the differences between the observed values and the predicted values).

Interpretation: This plot helps you check for linearity and homoscedasticity (equal variance of error terms). Ideally, you should see a horizontal red line (for linearity) and random scatter of points with no discernible pattern (for homoscedasticity). If there’s a pattern (e.g., a curve or fan shape), it suggests non-linearity or heteroscedasticity, which might indicate a problem with the model.

In the perfect model: points form an even band around 0 with no shape, and the red line stays flat. This is what “good” looks like.

In our case: the red line stays close to 0 but bends a little (slightly below 0 in the middle, rising above 0 at the highest fitted values), so there is mild nonlinearity. The bigger problem is the fan shape: the spread of residuals grows as fitted values grow, which breaks equal variance (Assumption 5). The residuals are also lopsided. Positive residuals reach about $14 million (sales 460, 565 and 11401), while negative residuals rarely go below $-2 million. In other words, the model badly underpredicts a few very expensive homes. Price data are often right skewed (long upper tail), and a log transformation of Y is a common fix.

What this plot CANNOT tell you — Assumption 4 (zero conditional mean). A flat red line here does not prove E[ε∣X]=0. By construction, OLS forces the residuals to average zero and to be uncorrelated with the included Xs — so the residual plot will look “fine” even when an important variable has been left out. Zero conditional mean is about research design and theory (did we include the right controls, is X exogenous?), not something a diagnostic plot can confirm. Omitted-variable bias cannot be detected by staring at residuals, and “more data never fixes it.”

Q–Q Plot

Q-Q plots helps us to compare a set of data with normal distribution. If the data is perfectly normally distributed, it should follow the dash line.

  • S-shaped curve: heavier tails or more peaked than the normal distribution (for example, a t-distribution).
  • Curved upward or downward: skewness (the data are not symmetric).
  • Clearly deviating from the straight line: Suggests the data are not normally distributed.
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # two plots side by side

# which = 2 gives the normal Q-Q plot of standardized residuals
plot(example_model, which = 2, main = "Perfect Model")
plot(simple_lm, which = 2, main = "Our Linear Model")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # reset the layout

In the perfect model: points follow the dashed line closely, with only small wiggles at the ends. That is normal sampling noise.

In our case: the left half of the points sits close to the line, but from about 1.5 theoretical quantiles the points curve sharply upward, reaching standardized residuals above 20 (sales 460, 11401 and 565). A normal distribution would almost never produce a value beyond 4. This one sided upward curve means the residuals are right skewed: a long upper tail of homes that sold for far more than the model predicts. Assumption 6 (normal errors) fails. With over 15,000 sales, p values are still roughly correct because of the central limit theorem, but the extreme tail is a warning about outliers.

Residuals vs Leverage

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # two plots side by side

# which = 5 gives Residuals vs Leverage with Cook's distance contours
plot(example_model, which = 5, main = "Perfect Model")
plot(simple_lm, which = 5, main = "Our Linear Model")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # reset the layout

Horizontal Axis: Leverage (hat values). Leverage measures how unusual an observation’s X values are, for example a very large or very old house. High leverage means a point could pull the line, but it does not mean it does.

Vertical Axis: Standardized residuals (residuals divided by their standard deviation).

Interpretation: This plot puts two ideas together. Points far above or below 0 are outliers (unusual Y given X). Points far to the right have high leverage (unusual X). A point is influential when it is both, which means removing it would move the regression line noticeably. The gray dashed curves are Cook’s distance contours at 0.5 and 1. Points beyond those curves (top right or bottom right corners) are the ones to worry about. If no curve shows up in the plot, every point is far inside them.

In the perfect model: residuals stay between about -2 and 2, and leverage is small and similar for everyone (equally spaced X). No Cook’s contour is visible.

In our case: most sales sit near zero leverage, as expected with 15,409 observations. Sale 460 has a huge residual (about 21) but low leverage, so it is an outlier with limited influence. Sale 11401 has both a large residual (about 19) and higher leverage (a 9,110 sqft house), so it sits close to the Cook’s distance = 0.5 contour (its Cook’s D is 0.46). Sale 13510 is similar but smaller. Nothing crosses 0.5, so no single sale is strongly changing the line. But are these sales errors, and should we remove them? The next section shows how to decide.

Outliers, Leverage and Influence: Should We Remove Them?

It is tempting to delete any point that looks unusual. That is usually a bad idea. A careful decision has two parts: metrics to flag rows, and judgment to decide what to do with them.

Step 1. Flag with metrics. Each metric answers a different question (n = number of observations, k = number of coefficients including the intercept):

Metric R function Question it answers Common cutoff
Studentized residual rstudent() Is Y unusual given X? (outlier) |r|>3
Leverage (hat value) hatvalues() Are the X values unusual? >2k/n or 3k/n
Cook’s distance cooks.distance() How much do all coefficients change if this row is dropped? >4/n: look; >0.5: investigate; >1: highly influential
DFBETAS dfbetas() How much does one coefficient change if this row is dropped? |DFBETAS|>2/n
Bonferroni outlier test car::outlierTest() Is the largest residual too big to be chance, after adjusting for many tests? Bonferroni p<0.05 
n <- nobs(simple_lm)          # number of observations used in the model
k <- length(coef(simple_lm))  # number of coefficients, including the intercept

# one row per sale with the three main influence measures
influence_lm <- data.frame(
  row      = 1:n,
  rstudent = rstudent(simple_lm),       # studentized residual
  leverage = hatvalues(simple_lm),      # hat value
  cooks_d  = cooks.distance(simple_lm)  # Cook's distance
)

# how many sales does each rule flag?
c(outlier_r3      = sum(abs(influence_lm$rstudent) > 3),
  leverage_3k_n   = sum(influence_lm$leverage > 3 * k / n),
  cooks_4_n       = sum(influence_lm$cooks_d > 4 / n),
  cooks_0.5       = sum(influence_lm$cooks_d > 0.5),
  dfbeta_sqft     = sum(abs(dfbetas(simple_lm)[, "sqft"]) > 2 / sqrt(n)))
##    outlier_r3 leverage_3k_n     cooks_4_n     cooks_0.5   dfbeta_sqft 
##           282           275           678             0           772

With n=15,409, the “4/n” cutoff is only 0.00026, so it flags 678 sales. The loose rules flag hundreds of rows in a large dataset. They tell us where to look, not what to delete. Only the 0.5 rule is strict, and it flags none.

Step 2. Look at the flagged rows. Is it a data error, or a real sale that the model cannot explain?

# the five most influential sales, with a few columns that describe them
top5 <- order(influence_lm$cooks_d, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
cbind(influence_lm[top5, c("rstudent", "cooks_d")],
      sales[top5, c("sale_price", "sqft", "year_built", "city", "wfnt", "sale_warning")])
##       rstudent    cooks_d sale_price sqft year_built         city wfnt
## 11401 18.93853 0.45594692   16518888 9110       2021       MEDINA    0
## 13510 11.13919 0.09104044   10750000 7390       2021       MEDINA    0
## 460   21.79158 0.08860685   16200000 4430       1962      SEATTLE    6
## 1087  15.12836 0.04103089   12000000 4340       1961 YARROW POINT    6
## 9752  14.96125 0.03984449   11880000 4600       1997       MEDINA    6
##       sale_warning
## 11401             
## 13510             
## 460               
## 1087              
## 9752

These are real luxury sales, not typos. Sales 11401 and 13510 are new mansions in Medina (over 7,000 sqft, built in 2021). Sales 460, 1087 and 9752 are on the Lake Washington waterfront (wfnt = 6 is the King County code for Lake Washington). None has an assessor sale warning (sale_warning is blank). They look like outliers because our model only knows size and age. It does not know about waterfront, location or lot size, which explain most of these prices.

Step 3. Sensitivity analysis. Refit the model without the flagged rows and see whether the conclusion changes.

# refit without the 3 sales with the largest Cook's distance
top3 <- order(influence_lm$cooks_d, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
lm_drop3 <- update(simple_lm, data = sales[-top3, ])

# refit without every sale above the 4/n cutoff (the "mechanical" approach)
lm_drop4n <- update(simple_lm, data = sales[influence_lm$cooks_d <= 4 / n, ])

# compare coefficients, R-squared and sample size side by side
data.frame(
  model = c("All sales", "Drop top 3", "Drop Cook's D > 4/n"),
  sqft = c(coef(simple_lm)["sqft"], coef(lm_drop3)["sqft"], coef(lm_drop4n)["sqft"]),
  year_built = c(coef(simple_lm)["year_built"], coef(lm_drop3)["year_built"],
                 coef(lm_drop4n)["year_built"]),
  r_squared = c(summary(simple_lm)$r.squared, summary(lm_drop3)$r.squared,
                summary(lm_drop4n)$r.squared),
  n = c(nobs(simple_lm), nobs(lm_drop3), nobs(lm_drop4n))
)
##                 model     sqft year_built r_squared     n
## 1           All sales 501.0786  -4022.477 0.3167381 15409
## 2          Drop top 3 488.4522  -3957.888 0.3179086 15406
## 3 Drop Cook's D > 4/n 446.8977  -2304.808 0.4916941 14731
# median price of the sales the 4/n rule would delete, vs all sales
median(sales$sale_price[influence_lm$cooks_d > 4 / n])
## [1] 3149000
median(sales$sale_price)
## [1] 895000

Dropping the top three changes the sqft slope only a little (about $501 to $488 per sqft). Dropping all 678 rows above 4/n raises R-squared from 0.32 to 0.49, which looks like a better model. But the deleted sales have a median price of about $3.1 million, versus $895,000 overall. We did not improve the model; we removed the expensive part of the market and changed the population we describe.

Step 4. Decide and report.

  • Remove a row only if it is a data error (impossible values, duplicate records, a sale price of $1) or it is outside the population you want to study (for example, a sale between family members, which is not an arm’s length market sale).
  • Keep a real observation that the model cannot explain. Fix the model instead: transform Y (log), add missing variables, or use a method that is less sensitive to extreme values (robust regression).
  • Report what you did. If you remove rows, say how many, why, and show that the key results do not depend on the choice.

Our decision: keep these sales. They are real, they pass the strict Cook’s D<0.5 rule, and the sensitivity check shows the slope barely moves. Their large residuals point to a missing variable problem and a skewed Y, which we address next with a log transformation.

Multicollinearity

The Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) measures how much the variance of a regression coefficient is inflated due to collinearity with other predictors. If there is perfect multicollinearity, R will automatically drop one of the variables. If there is imperfect multicollinearity. R won’t drop and the model estimates will be biased.

  • VIF = 1: no correlation with other predictors.
  • VIF > 5: moderate multicollinearity concern, potential for removal.
  • VIF > 10: serious multicollinearity, must remove the variable
#install.packages('car') # run once
library(car)  # Companion to Applied Regression: diagnostics such as vif()
## Warning: package 'car' was built under R version 4.6.2
## Warning: package 'carData' was built under R version 4.6.2
# variance inflation factor for each X in the model
vif(simple_lm)
##       sqft year_built 
##   1.095851   1.095851

Independence of Errors

Assumption 2 says the residuals should be independent of each other. With housing sales this is often violated in two ways: sales close in time can share market shocks, and sales close in space (same block or neighborhood) tend to have similar unobserved quality. When errors are correlated, the standard errors can be half their true size, so noise looks significant.

A quick temporal check is the Durbin–Watson test (also in the car package). The statistic ranges from 0 to 4; a value near 2 means no autocorrelation, below 2 suggests positive autocorrelation, and a small p-value flags a problem.

# Durbin-Watson version (can be slow on large data, so we leave it commented out)
# order the data by sale_date first so "neighboring" rows are adjacent in time
installed.packages("car")
##      Package LibPath Version Priority Depends Imports LinkingTo Suggests
##      Enhances License License_is_FOSS License_restricts_use OS_type Archs
##      MD5sum NeedsCompilation Built Published
library(car)
durbinWatsonTest(lm(sale_price ~ sqft + year_built,
                     data = sales[order(sales$sale_date), ]))
##  lag Autocorrelation D-W Statistic p-value
##    1       0.1761858      1.647614       0
##  Alternative hypothesis: rho != 0
library(lmtest)  # tests for linear models, including bgtest()
## Warning: package 'lmtest' was built under R version 4.6.2
# refit the same model on data sorted by sale date,
# so "next row" means "next sale in time"
model <- lm(sale_price ~ sqft + year_built, data = sales[order(sales$sale_date), ])

# Breusch-Godfrey test for serial correlation (handles large data well)
# H0: no autocorrelation; order = 1 checks each residual against the previous one
bgtest(model, order = 1)
## 
##  Breusch-Godfrey test for serial correlation of order up to 1
## 
## data:  model
## LM test = 479.66, df = 1, p-value < 2.2e-16
# the same idea by hand: correlation between each residual and the next one
res <- residuals(model)
cor(res[-length(res)], res[-1]) # drop last / drop first so the two vectors line up
## [1] 0.1761871

In our case: the Breusch–Godfrey test has a p value below 2.2e-16, and the correlation between each residual and the next one (in time order) is about 0.18. Sales close in time do share some of their errors.

Spatial Autocorrelation: Moran’s I

For spatial dependence, the standard tool is Moran’s I computed on the model residuals. It asks: are the residuals of nearby homes more similar than we would expect by chance?

  • I≈0 (more precisely, close to −1/(n−1)): no spatial pattern.
  • I>0: nearby homes have similar residuals (positive spatial autocorrelation). This is the common case for housing.
  • I<0: nearby homes have opposite residuals (rare in practice).

Moran’s I needs a spatial weights matrix that defines who is a “neighbor” of whom. With polygons (census tracts, counties), we often use shared borders (queen or rook contiguity). With points, like our sales with latitude and longitude, we define neighbors by distance instead:

  • k nearest neighbors: each sale’s k closest sales (e.g. k=8). Every sale gets the same number of neighbors, so this is a common choice for point data.
  • Distance band: every sale within, say, 1 km. Easy to explain, but sales in rural areas may end up with no neighbors.
  • Inverse distance: all sales count, but closer ones count more.
#install.packages("spdep") # run once
library(spdep)  # spatial dependence: weights, Moran's I, spatial models

# coordinates as a two column matrix: longitude (x) first, then latitude (y)
coords <- cbind(sales$longitude, sales$latitude)

# find each sale's 8 nearest sales
# longlat = TRUE measures great circle distance in km (right for lat/long)
# (R warns about "identical points": some homes sold more than once in 2023,
#  or condos share one building location; knearneigh() still handles them)
knn8 <- knearneigh(coords, k = 8, longlat = TRUE)
nb8  <- knn2nb(knn8)  # convert to a neighbor list

# turn the neighbor list into weights
# style = "W" (row standardized): each sale's 8 neighbors get weight 1/8
lw8 <- nb2listw(nb8, style = "W")

# Moran's I test on the residuals of our linear model
# H0: no spatial autocorrelation in the residuals
lm.morantest(simple_lm, lw8)
## 
##  Global Moran I for regression residuals
## 
## data:  
## model: lm(formula = sale_price ~ sqft + year_built, data = sales)
## weights: lw8
## 
## Moran I statistic standard deviate = 132.14, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: greater
## sample estimates:
## Observed Moran I      Expectation         Variance 
##     5.013768e-01    -1.235376e-04     1.440263e-05

In our case: Moran’s I is about 0.50, far above its expected value under no autocorrelation (about 0), and the p value is essentially zero. This is strong positive spatial autocorrelation: when the model underpredicts one home, it tends to underpredict its neighbors too. This matches what we saw with the outliers. The very expensive Medina and Lake Washington waterfront sales were not random misses; they were missed together, because the model does not know about location.

The value of I depends on how we define neighbors, so it is good practice to check a few choices:

# repeat the test with 4, 8 and 12 neighbors (this takes a little while)
# the names k4, k8, k12 label the output
sapply(c(k4 = 4, k8 = 8, k12 = 12), function(k) {
  lw_k <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = k, longlat = TRUE)), style = "W")
  unname(lm.morantest(simple_lm, lw_k)$estimate["Observed Moran I"]) # keep only Moran's I
})
##        k4        k8       k12 
## 0.5228025 0.5013768 0.4868114

Moran’s I stays around 0.49 to 0.52 for 4, 8 and 12 neighbors, so the conclusion does not depend on that choice.

What Can We Do About Correlated Errors?

We have now found both temporal autocorrelation (Breusch–Godfrey) and spatial autocorrelation (Moran’s I). This breaks Assumption 2 (independent errors). What does that mean for our results?

What still stands

  • The coefficient estimates, if the only problem is correlated errors. If X is still unrelated to the error (Assumption 4 holds), OLS slopes stay unbiased. The line is still right on average.
  • R-squared and the fitted values as a description of the data.

What does not stand

  • Standard errors, t values, p values and confidence intervals. With positive autocorrelation, nearby sales carry partly the same information, so we have less independent information than 15,409 sales suggest. The usual standard errors are too small, the confidence intervals are too narrow, and the significance stars look more convincing than they should.
  • “Best” (BLUE). OLS is no longer the most precise estimator (Gauss–Markov needs independent errors).
  • Be careful with the first point. Spatial autocorrelation in the residuals is often a symptom of a missing variable (location, neighborhood quality, waterfront, views). If that missing variable is also related to X (bigger houses are more common in Medina), Assumption 4 fails too, and then the coefficients themselves are biased, not just their standard errors.

What we can do (we will not run these here)

Approach Idea Fixes standard errors? Fixes biased coefficients?
Robust standard errors Keep the OLS estimates, recompute the standard errors to allow correlation: Newey–West (time), clustered by neighborhood or submarket, or Conley (spatial) Yes No
Add the missing variables Location fixed effects (city, submarket, census tract), time fixed effects (month of sale), waterfront and view variables Often reduces the problem Yes, if the missing variable was the cause
Model the dependence directly Spatial lag or spatial error models, multilevel (neighborhood) models, time series models Yes Depends on the model

The order usually matters: first ask why the errors are correlated. If something important is missing from the model, add it. Robust standard errors are a good second step, because they give honest uncertainty but cannot fix a wrong slope. (We will revisit spatial methods later in the course.)

Adjustment to the Regression

Because the original model showed heteroscedasticity (the “fan shape” pattern in residual plots), we apply a log transformation to the Y sale_price. The log compresses the long upper tail of prices, so the very expensive homes are no longer so extreme.

# refit the model with log(sale_price) as Y
log_simple_lm <- lm(data = sales, log(sale_price) ~ sqft + year_built)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))  # 2 x 2 grid: all four default diagnostic plots in one figure
plot(log_simple_lm)   # with no "which", plot() draws the four standard panels

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))  # reset the layout

Reading the four panels (compare each with the same plot for simple_lm):

  • Residuals vs Fitted (top left): the fan shape is mostly gone. Residuals now spread fairly evenly between about -1.5 and 2 on the log scale. The red line is flat for most homes but bends down for the few homes with fitted values above 15 (predicted prices above about $3.3 million). The model now slightly overpredicts these.
  • Q–Q Residuals (top right): much closer to the line than before (the largest standardized residual drops from about 21 to about 6). Both tails still bend away, giving a mild S shape: the errors have heavier tails than a normal distribution, especially on the upper side. Better, but not perfectly normal.
  • Scale–Location (bottom left): this new panel plots the square root of the absolute standardized residuals against fitted values. A flat red line means equal variance. Here it rises at the low end, stays flat in the middle and creeps up again at the high end, so some unequal variance remains, but far less than before.
  • Residuals vs Leverage (bottom right): no Cook’s distance contour is visible, so every sale is far below 0.5 (the largest Cook’s D is about 0.02). Sales 10189 and 1183 have the highest leverage (two very large houses), but their residuals are moderate. Sale 460, the biggest outlier before, still stands out (about 5) but is no longer extreme.

Summary: the log transformation fixes most of the unequal variance and removes the extreme influence, and the residuals are much closer to normal. It does not make the model perfect; the remaining heavy tails suggest that important variables (location, waterfront) are still missing.

summary(log_simple_lm) # coefficients are now on the log price scale
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = log(sale_price) ~ sqft + year_built, data = sales)
## 
## Residuals:
##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
## -2.20895 -0.27047 -0.02287  0.22047  2.57397 
## 
## Coefficients:
##               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)  1.785e+01  2.008e-01   88.90   <2e-16 ***
## sqft         3.688e-04  3.660e-06  100.78   <2e-16 ***
## year_built  -2.450e-03  1.027e-04  -23.86   <2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.3983 on 15406 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.3982, Adjusted R-squared:  0.3981 
## F-statistic:  5097 on 2 and 15406 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

You may notice that the β in log-transformed model is quite small. Because of the transformation, our interpretation of β could be different! Holding other variables constant, we change X1 for one unit, we can write as:

log⁡(Ychanged)=β0+β1(X1+1)+β2X2+ε=β0+β1X1+β2X2+ε+β1=log⁡(Yoriginal)+β1β1=log⁡(Ychanged)−log⁡(Yoriginal)=log⁡(YchangedYoriginal)exp⁡(β1)=YchangedYoriginal

We use coef() to get accurate β:

coef(log_simple_lm) # print the coefficients with full precision
##   (Intercept)          sqft    year_built 
## 17.8549237079  0.0003688245 -0.0024502564
# exp(beta) = ratio of new price to old price for a one sqft increase
exp(0.0003717023)
## [1] 1.000372

So, we can explain the relationship between sale price and square footage of house as: holding all year variables constant, the expected percentage change in price for 1 sqft increase is 0.3%.

Note: if we want to know expected percentage change in price for 100 sqft, it should be 1.000372100 (+3.79%) instead of 0.000372×100 (+3.72%).

Interactions and Non-linear Variables

An interaction means that the effect of one variable depends on the level of another variable. For example, we may think of the effect of house size on price changes depending on the house’s condition. We can add interaction terms by using *. Note: R will add condition itself as an explanatory variable in the following model:

# model without interaction: the effect of sqft is the same for every condition
log_no_interaction_lm <- lm(data = sales, log(sale_price) ~ year_built + sqft + condition)

# model with interaction: sqft * condition adds sqft, condition AND sqft:condition,
# so the effect of sqft can change with the condition of the house
log_interaction_lm <- lm(data = sales, log(sale_price) ~ year_built + sqft + sqft * condition)

You could also have variables in you specification that are squared, cubed etc. such as:

# I(sqft^2) adds a squared term; cos(sqft) shows any function of X can be used
model7 <- lm(sale_price ~  sqft + I(sqft^2) + cos(sqft), data = sales)

The I() is a base R command that forces R to evaluate anything inside the I() before anything else. Sometimes it is needed when conducting regressions.

Compare Models

When compare with several models, we can use modelsummary package to display and compare regression results in one formatted table. It helps us quickly see how coefficients, significance levels, and model fit change.

# put both models in one table, one column per model
modelsummary(
  list(
    "Without Interaction Model" = log_no_interaction_lm,
    "Interaction Model" = log_interaction_lm
  ),
  stars = TRUE,  # add significance stars
  fmt = 5,       # show 5 decimal places (log coefficients are small)
  title = 'Comparison Table between Models with/without Interaction',
  output = "html")
Comparison Table between Models with/without Interaction
Without Interaction Model Interaction Model
+ p < 0.1, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001
(Intercept) 17.99260*** 18.12357***
(0.22241) (0.22250)
year_built -0.00251*** -0.00243***
(0.00011) (0.00011)
sqft 0.00037*** 0.00023***
(0.00000) (0.00002)
condition -0.00662 -0.08810***
(0.00459) (0.01089)
sqft × condition 0.00004***
(0.00000)
Num.Obs. 15409 15409
R2 0.398 0.401
R2 Adj. 0.398 0.401
AIC 440451.9 440386.0
BIC 440490.1 440431.9
Log.Lik. -7678.494 -7644.564
F 3399.128 2577.429
RMSE 0.40 0.40

In an interaction model, the β of individual variables (those also appearing in the interaction term) represent their effects only when the other interacting variable equals zero. So, it is a baseline effect and does not have much direct meanings. We must always interpret them together with the interaction term. In our interaction model:

  • 0.00026: effect of sqft when condition = 0 (condition cannot be 0 in the data)
  • -0.06512: effect of condition when sqft = 0 (square footage of house is not likely to be 0)

For the interaction term, we can explain as: with a one-unit increase in condition, holding other variables constant, the coefficient (slope) of sqft increases by 0.0003.

We see a significant positive interaction: the positive effect of square footage on price is stronger for houses in better condition. In other words, larger houses benefit more from good condition than smaller ones.

Performance Metrics

R-squared and Adjusted R-squared [larger - better]: Mentioned in the lecture, R-squared shows how much of the variation in the response variable is explained by the model. Adjusted R-squared corrects for the number of predictors, so it is better for comparing models with different numbers of variables.

Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) [smaller - better]: Root of MSE, measures the average distance between the observed and predicted values. Smaller RMSE means better model fit.

Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC) [smaller - better]: AIC is good for unknown data generating process(The AIC tries to select the model that most adequately describes an unknown, high dimensional reality. Akaike’s Information Criteria is good for making asymptotically equivalent to cross-validation. You can check AIC using AIC(model).

Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) [smaller - better]: BIC tries to find the TRUE model among the set of candidates. A lot of times, BIC and AIC will agrees on each other, but BIC penalize models that have a lot of parameters. Danger of underfit. Bayesian Information Criteria is good for consistent estimation. You can check BIC using BIC(model).

In general, our interaction model perform better in terms of all four metrics. And we will use this model to conduct prediction. Note: we may still need same assumption check for the new model.

Prediction

We can use predict function to generate predicted values from a regression model.

# predict() returns the fitted value for each row of newdata
# note: the argument is "newdata" (an argument called "data" would be ignored)
sales$predicted <- predict(log_interaction_lm, newdata = sales)

# look at the prediction for the first sale
sales$predicted[1]
##        1 
## 13.57456

Check the prediction, we find the value is extremely small (13.57 << real sale price). We used log transformation to response variable! We need to transform the predicted values back by taking the exponential (exp) of each prediction to return them to the original sale price scale.

# undo the log: exp(log(price)) = price
sales$predicted_exp <- exp(sales$predicted)
sales$predicted_exp[1]
##        1 
## 785876.9

A Logistic Regression

So far our Y (sale price) is a continuous number. Many questions in real estate have a yes or no answer instead. Was the mortgage application denied? Did the household move? Did the property sell within 30 days? For a binary Y (1/0), we use logistic regression.

The HMDA Data

We use the HMDA dataset from the AER package (Applied Econometrics with R). It comes from the well known Boston Fed study by Munnell et al. (1996), Mortgage Lending in Boston: Interpreting HMDA Data (American Economic Review), which used Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA) records plus extra information collected from lenders. Each row is one mortgage application in the Boston area in 1990 (N=2,380). The study asked whether race was associated with mortgage denial after accounting for the applicant’s credit and financial profile.

Key variables we use (see ?HMDA for the full list):

Variable Meaning
deny Response: was the mortgage denied? (no/yes)
pirat Payment to income ratio (total monthly debt / income)
hirat Housing expense to income ratio
lvrat Loan to value ratio (loan amount / property value)
chist Consumer credit score, 1 (best) to 6 (worst)
mhist Mortgage credit score, 1 (best) to 4 (worst)
phist Public bad credit record? (no/yes)
selfemp Is the applicant self employed? (no/yes)
insurance Was the applicant denied mortgage insurance? (no/yes)
afam Is the applicant African American? (no/yes) 
#install.packages("AER") # you only need to run the installation once
library(AER)   # Applied Econometrics with R: includes the HMDA data
## Warning: package 'AER' was built under R version 4.6.2
## Warning: package 'sandwich' was built under R version 4.6.2
data(HMDA)     # load the mortgage application data

# make a 0/1 version of the response for plotting and summaries
# (glm() can use the yes/no factor directly; the 0/1 copy is for our own plots and means)
hmda <- HMDA %>%
  mutate(deny01 = ifelse(deny == "yes", 1, 0))
head(hmda)     # look at the first six rows
##   deny pirat hirat     lvrat chist mhist phist unemp selfemp insurance condomin
## 1   no 0.221 0.221 0.8000000     5     2    no   3.9      no        no       no
## 2   no 0.265 0.265 0.9218750     2     2    no   3.2      no        no       no
## 3   no 0.372 0.248 0.9203980     1     2    no   3.2      no        no       no
## 4   no 0.320 0.250 0.8604651     1     2    no   4.3      no        no       no
## 5   no 0.360 0.350 0.6000000     1     1    no   3.2      no        no       no
## 6   no 0.240 0.170 0.5105263     1     1    no   3.9      no        no       no
##   afam single hschool deny01
## 1   no     no     yes      0
## 2   no    yes     yes      0
## 3   no     no     yes      0
## 4   no     no     yes      0
## 5   no     no     yes      0
## 6   no     no     yes      0

Exploring the Data

With a binary Y, correlation and scatterplots are less helpful. Every point sits at 0 or 1. Instead, we look at the share of Y=1 across groups or across bins of X.

# overall denial rate: the mean of a 0/1 variable is the share of 1s
mean(hmda$deny01)
## [1] 0.1197479
# denial rate by race: count and share denied within each group
hmda %>%
  group_by(afam) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), deny_rate = mean(deny01))
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   afam      n deny_rate
##   <fct> <int>     <dbl>
## 1 no     2041    0.0926
## 2 yes     339    0.283

About 12% of all applications were denied. The raw denial rate is 28.3% for African American applicants and 9.3% for other applicants. This is a raw gap. It does not yet account for credit history, debt or loan size.

ggplot(hmda, aes(x = pirat, y = deny01)) +
  # jitter moves points up/down a little so the 0s and 1s do not sit on top of each other
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, size = 0.5, alpha = 0.4, color = "#85754d") +
  # fit a one variable logistic regression and draw its S shaped curve with a 95% band
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = binomial),
              formula = y ~ x, color = "#4b2e83", linewidth = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +  # zoom in without dropping data from the fit
  labs(x = "Payment to Income Ratio (pirat)",
       y = "Denied (1) or Approved (0)",
       title = "Mortgage Denial vs. Payment to Income Ratio") +
  theme_minimal()

Reading the plot: each dot is one application, placed at 1 (denied, top band) or 0 (approved, bottom band) and jittered so they do not overlap. Most applicants have pirat between 0.2 and 0.45, so the bottom band is very dense there. The purple line is a one variable logistic fit. It is an S shape that stays between 0 and 1. The predicted denial probability is below 10% for ratios under about 0.3, then climbs quickly: about 25% at a ratio of 0.5 and about 60% at 0.75. The gray band (95% confidence interval) is narrow where data are dense and very wide above 0.5, where we only have a few applicants. (We zoom in to pirat ≤1; a few extreme values go up to 3.)

Why Not a Linear Model?

We can run lm() on a 0/1 outcome. This is called a linear probability model (LPM). But look at the fitted values:

# linear probability model: plain OLS on the 0/1 outcome
lpm <- lm(deny01 ~ pirat + afam, data = hmda)

# smallest and largest predicted "probability"
range(fitted(lpm))
## [1] -0.0905136  1.5870702

Some predicted “probabilities” are below 0 and some are above 1. That makes no sense. The LPM also breaks the equal variance assumption by design: for a 0/1 outcome, Var(Y∣X)=P(1−P), which changes with X. Logistic regression solves both problems.

The Logistic Model

Let P=P(Y=1∣X). Instead of modeling P directly, we model the log odds (also called the logit):

log⁡(P1−P)=β0+β1X1+β2X2+…

  • Odds =P1−P. If P=0.2, the odds are 0.2/0.8=0.25 (1 denial for every 4 approvals).
  • The right side is still a linear combination of X, just like OLS.
  • We can solve back for the probability: P=exp⁡(β0+β1X1+…)1+exp⁡(β0+β1X1+…), which always stays between 0 and 1.

The model is estimated by maximum likelihood, not least squares. In R, we use glm() (generalized linear model) with family = binomial.

Fitting the Model

We start with a simple model, then a fuller model with the credit and loan controls.

# glm() = generalized linear model
# family = binomial tells R the outcome is yes/no and to use the logit link
logit_simple <- glm(deny ~ pirat + afam, data = hmda, family = binomial)
summary(logit_simple)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = deny ~ pirat + afam, family = binomial, data = hmda)
## 
## Coefficients:
##             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)  -4.1256     0.2684 -15.370  < 2e-16 ***
## pirat         5.3704     0.7283   7.374 1.66e-13 ***
## afamyes       1.2728     0.1462   8.706  < 2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 1744.2  on 2379  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance: 1591.4  on 2377  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 1597.4
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5
# add credit history and loan controls
# chist and mhist are factors, so R creates one dummy per level (except the reference)
logit_full <- glm(deny ~ pirat + hirat + lvrat + chist + mhist + phist +
                    selfemp + insurance + afam,
                  data = hmda, family = binomial)
summary(logit_full)
##

## AIC: 1305.3

How to read the glm() table? Most parts look like the lm() table, with a few differences:

  • Estimate: the change in the log odds of Y=1 for a one unit increase in X, holding other variables constant. The sign tells the direction. The size is hard to read directly.
  • z value: estimate divided by standard error. It plays the same role as the t value in lm(). The test is H0:β=0.
  • Pr(>|z|): the p value for that test.
  • Null deviance vs. Residual deviance: deviance measures how badly the model fits (−2× log likelihood). The null deviance is for a model with only the intercept. A large drop means the Xs help.
  • There is no R-squared and no residual standard error. We use AIC, BIC and pseudo R-squared instead (see below).

From Log Odds to Odds Ratios

Log odds are not intuitive, so we usually report odds ratios. Like the log transformation in the linear model, we take exp() of β:

log⁡(oddschanged)−log⁡(oddsoriginal)=β1exp⁡(β1)=oddschangedoddsoriginal

# coef() gives log odds; exp() turns them into odds ratios
# confint() on a glm gives profile likelihood intervals; exp() puts them on the OR scale
# cbind() glues the columns together into one table
exp(cbind(OR = coef(logit_simple), confint(logit_simple)))
## Waiting for profiling to be done...
##                       OR        2.5 %       97.5 %
## (Intercept)   0.01615448  0.009392082   0.02687566
## pirat       214.94067334 53.848128122 931.65749990
## afamyes       3.57077239  2.674741842   4.74680906

How to read an odds ratio (OR):

  • OR =1: no association.
  • OR >1: higher odds of Y=1. OR =1.5 means 50% higher odds.
  • OR <1: lower odds of Y=1. OR =0.8 means 20% lower odds.
  • If the 95% confidence interval of the OR contains 1, the variable is not significant at the 5% level.

In our case: in logit_simple, the OR for afamyes is about 3.57 (95% CI: 2.67 to 4.75). Holding the payment to income ratio constant, African American applicants have about 3.6 times the odds of denial. The OR for pirat is huge (about 215) because a one unit change in pirat (from 0 to 1, i.e. 0% to 100% of income) is a very large change. A 0.1 increase is more meaningful: exp⁡(5.37×0.1)≈1.71, so 71% higher odds of denial. This is the same idea as the 100 sqft example in the linear model.

Odds are not probabilities. “3.6 times the odds” does not mean “3.6 times as likely”. When the outcome is rare (say below 10%), the two are close. When it is common, they can be very different. We will convert results to probabilities in the Prediction section.

Check Assumptions of Logistic Regression

Logistic regression has fewer assumptions than OLS, but they are different. Compare with the six OLS assumptions above:

OLS assumption Logistic regression
1. Linearity in Y Linearity in the log odds for each continuous X
2. Independent errors Still required: independent observations
3. No perfect collinearity Still required: check VIF
4. Zero conditional mean Still required: no omitted confounders (design, not a plot)
5. Equal variance Not required: variance is P(1−P) by design
6. Normal errors Not required: Y follows a binomial (Bernoulli) distribution
(new) Binary outcome, no extreme influential points, large enough sample and no (quasi) separation

Because assumptions 5 and 6 are not required, the Q–Q plot from plot(model) is not meaningful for logistic regression. The residuals of a 0/1 outcome are never normal. Do not use it.

Binary Outcome

The response must have exactly two categories. deny is a factor with levels no and yes. R models the probability of the second level (yes), so check the level order.

levels(hmda$deny) # R models P(second level), here P(deny = "yes")
## [1] "no"  "yes"
table(hmda$deny)  # how many of each outcome
## 
##   no  yes 
## 2095  285

Linearity in the Log Odds

Logistic regression does not need Y to be linear in X. It needs the log odds to be linear in each continuous X. A simple check is the empirical logit plot: cut X into bins (here 10 equal sized groups), compute the share of denials in each bin, and convert it to log odds. If the points follow a straight line, the assumption is fine.

emp_logit <- hmda %>%
  # stack pirat and lvrat into one column so we can treat them the same way
  pivot_longer(cols = c(pirat, lvrat), names_to = "variable", values_to = "xvalue") %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  mutate(bin = ntile(xvalue, 10)) %>%   # cut each X into 10 groups of equal size
  group_by(variable, bin) %>%
  summarise(x_mean = mean(xvalue),       # middle of the bin
            p = mean(deny01),            # share denied in the bin
            log_odds = log(p / (1 - p)), # convert the share to log odds
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(emp_logit, aes(x = x_mean, y = log_odds)) +
  geom_point(color = "#4b2e83", size = 2) +              # one point per bin
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, # straight reference line
              color = "#b7a57a", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Mean of X within Bin", y = "Empirical Log Odds of Denial",
       title = "Empirical Logit Plot (10 Bins)") +
  theme_minimal()

In our case:

  • lvrat (left panel): the points rise from about -3.2 to -1.0 and follow the dashed line fairly well. The two bins in the middle are a bit noisy, and the highest bin sits above the line, but there is no clear curve. Roughly linear.
  • pirat (right panel): the pattern is not a straight line. The lowest bin (mean ratio about 0.18) has higher log odds than the next few bins, then the points are flat around -2.5, and the highest bin (mean about 0.5) jumps to about -0.5. This is a J shape. The effect of debt is not constant: it matters little in the normal range and a lot once the ratio gets high. (The slightly higher denial rate at very low ratios may reflect applicants with unusual or incomplete income records.)

A formal check is the Box–Tidwell test. We add X×log⁡(X) for each continuous X. If that extra term is significant, the log odds are not linear in X. (It needs X>0, so we drop a few zero values.)

# log(X) needs X > 0, so drop the few rows with a zero ratio
bt_data <- hmda %>% filter(pirat > 0, hirat > 0, lvrat > 0)

# Box-Tidwell: add X * log(X) for each continuous X we want to test
box_tidwell <- glm(deny ~ pirat + I(pirat * log(pirat)) + hirat +
                     lvrat + I(lvrat * log(lvrat)) + chist + mhist +
                     phist + selfemp + insurance + afam,
                   data = bt_data, family = binomial)
## Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
# show only the two test terms: a small p value means the logit is NOT linear in that X
coef(summary(box_tidwell))[c("I(pirat * log(pirat))", "I(lvrat * log(lvrat))"), ]
##                        Estimate Std. Error   z value   Pr(>|z|)
## I(pirat * log(pirat)) 6.6649542   2.846868 2.3411533 0.01922427
## I(lvrat * log(lvrat)) 0.7093261   1.808486 0.3922209 0.69489501

The pirat term is significant (p ≈ 0.02) but the lvrat term is not (p ≈ 0.69). This confirms the plot: pirat needs some adjustment. You may also see the warning fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred. That is a hint of a few extreme points, which we check next.

Influential Points

Just like the linear model, a few unusual applications can pull the estimates. plot(model, which = 4) shows Cook’s distance and which = 5 shows residuals vs leverage. Both work for glm().

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))         # two plots side by side
plot(logit_full, which = 4)  # Cook's distance for every application
plot(logit_full, which = 5)  # standardized Pearson residuals vs leverage

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))         # reset the layout
# look at the three rows labeled in the plots
hmda[c(801, 1321, 412), c("deny", "pirat", "hirat", "lvrat", "insurance")]
##      deny pirat hirat     lvrat insurance
## 801    no  0.22  0.19 1.9500000       yes
## 1321   no  1.28  0.73 0.7075472        no
## 412    no  0.95  0.44 0.5470588        no
# how many applications have debt payments larger than income?
sum(hmda$pirat > 1)
## [1] 5

Reading the plots:

  • Cook’s distance (left): one spike per application. The largest values are rows 801 (about 0.044), 1321 (0.029) and 412 (0.025). All are far below 0.5. Most applications are close to 0.
  • Residuals vs Leverage (right): the points form two curved bands. This always happens with a 0/1 outcome. The upper band is the denied applicants (positive residuals), the lower band is the approved ones (negative residuals). Do not read the bands as a problem. Row 801 has the most extreme residual (about -7): the model gave it a very high chance of denial, but it was approved. Rows 1321 and 412 have the highest leverage of the labeled points because their debt ratios are extreme. The Cook’s 0.5 contours sit far away in the corners, so no point is highly influential.

What are these rows? Row 1321 has a payment to income ratio of 1.28, meaning monthly debt payments are larger than income. Five applications have pirat >1, and one has pirat =3. These are very likely data entry errors. Row 801 is different: its loan to value ratio is 1.95 (a loan almost twice the home value), and it was denied mortgage insurance but still approved. Only 4 of the 48 applicants denied insurance were approved, which is why the model is so surprised.

Should We Remove the Flagged Applications?

We follow the same four steps as in the linear model (see the table of metrics there). For glm(), rstandard(model, type = "pearson") gives the standardized Pearson residuals shown in the plot.

n_g <- nobs(logit_full)          # number of applications
k_g <- length(coef(logit_full))  # number of coefficients

cooks_g <- cooks.distance(logit_full)  # Cook's distance for each application

# Step 1: how many rows does each rule flag?
c(pearson_r3    = sum(abs(rstandard(logit_full, type = "pearson")) > 3),
  leverage_3k_n = sum(hatvalues(logit_full) > 3 * k_g / n_g),
  cooks_4_n     = sum(cooks_g > 4 / n_g),
  cooks_0.5     = sum(cooks_g > 0.5))
##    pearson_r3 leverage_3k_n     cooks_4_n     cooks_0.5 
##            74           170           215             0

The pattern is the same as before: the loose rules flag many rows (215 above 4/n), and the strict rule flags none.

# Step 3: sensitivity analysis, refit under three choices
logit_no_pirat1 <- update(logit_full, data = hmda[hmda$pirat <= 1, ]) # drop pirat > 1
logit_no_801    <- update(logit_full, data = hmda[-801, ])            # drop row 801
logit_no_4n     <- update(logit_full, data = hmda[cooks_g <= 4 / n_g, ]) # drop all 215
## Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
# compare the odds ratios of a few key variables across the four fits
round(rbind(
  "All rows"            = exp(coef(logit_full)),
  "Drop pirat > 1"      = exp(coef(logit_no_pirat1)),
  "Drop row 801"        = exp(coef(logit_no_801)),
  "Drop Cook's D > 4/n" = exp(coef(logit_no_4n))
)[, c("pirat", "lvrat", "insuranceyes", "afamyes")], 2)
##                         pirat lvrat insuranceyes afamyes
## All rows               169.90  5.91 9.602000e+01    1.98
## Drop pirat > 1         251.83  5.87 9.611000e+01    1.98
## Drop row 801           152.67  7.90 1.329100e+02    2.02
## Drop Cook's D > 4/n 109077.57 44.93 9.500794e+14    4.30

What the sensitivity analysis shows:

  • Dropping the five rows with pirat >1 mainly changes the pirat odds ratio (from about 170 to 252). The other odds ratios barely move.
  • Dropping row 801 raises the odds ratios for lvrat and insurance, because this one approved applicant with a huge loan to value ratio and an insurance denial was “pulling them down”. The afamyes odds ratio stays about 2.0.
  • Dropping all 215 rows above 4/n breaks the model. R warns fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred, the insurance odds ratio explodes to an absurd number, and the afamyes odds ratio doubles to 4.3. Deleting the applications the model fits worst leaves data that are too “clean”, close to perfect separation. Never delete rows only because a rule of thumb flags them.

Our decision:

  • Remove the five applications with pirat >1. Payments larger than income are almost certainly recording errors, and they are outside the population of realistic mortgage applicants.
  • Keep row 801, but note it. A loan to value ratio of 1.95 is unusual, but we cannot confirm it is an error, and our key variable (afamyes) does not depend on it. In the adjusted model below, we also group lvrat into categories, so this single extreme value no longer has extra leverage.
  • Report both choices and the sensitivity table.

Multicollinearity

VIF works the same way for glm(). When a model has factors with more than two levels (like chist), car::vif() reports a generalized VIF (GVIF). Use the last column, GVIF1/(2⋅Df), and square it to compare with the usual cutoffs of 5 and 10.

# for factors with several levels, car::vif() reports GVIF
# square the last column, GVIF^(1/(2*Df)), to compare with the usual 5 and 10 cutoffs
vif(logit_full)
##               GVIF Df GVIF^(1/(2*Df))
## pirat     1.866373  1        1.366153
## hirat     1.885874  1        1.373271
## lvrat     1.066973  1        1.032944
## chist     1.305852  5        1.027045
## mhist     1.194401  3        1.030050
## phist     1.119974  1        1.058288
## selfemp   1.054616  1        1.026945
## insurance 1.018724  1        1.009318
## afam      1.097189  1        1.047468

In our case: all values are below 2. pirat and hirat are correlated (housing costs are part of total debt), but not enough to be a problem.

Independence of Observations

Each application should be a separate draw. Here each row is a different applicant, so this is more reasonable than our housing sales data. But applications to the same bank or in the same neighborhood may share unobserved factors (lender policies, local market). The fix is the same as in the linear model: clustered or robust standard errors. Durbin–Watson is not used here because the data have no time order.

Sample Size and Separation

Logistic regression uses maximum likelihood, which needs a large enough sample. A common rule of thumb is at least 10 events per variable (EPV): the number of the rarer outcome divided by the number of coefficients (excluding the intercept).

# events per variable = number of denials / number of slopes (intercept excluded)
sum(hmda$deny01) / (length(coef(logit_full)) - 1)
## [1] 19

We have 285 denials and 15 coefficients, so EPV ≈ 19. That is fine.

Separation happens when an X (or a group of Xs) predicts Y perfectly. The estimate then runs off toward infinity, and R gives the warning fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred. Check cross tables for binary Xs:

# cross table: are there cells with (almost) no observations?
table(insurance = hmda$insurance, deny = hmda$deny)
##          deny
## insurance   no  yes
##       no  2091  241
##       yes    4   44
# the odds ratio for insurance denial
exp(coef(logit_full)["insuranceyes"])
## insuranceyes 
##     96.02495

Of the 48 applicants denied mortgage insurance, 44 were also denied the mortgage. This is close to separation. That is why its odds ratio is about 96 with a large standard error. It is not perfect separation, so the model still runs, but we should read this coefficient with care.

Binned Residual Plot

The Residuals vs Fitted plot from plot(model, which = 1) is hard to read for 0/1 data. You always see two curved bands of points. A better tool is the binned residual plot (Gelman and Hill, 2007). We sort observations by predicted probability, cut them into bins, and plot the average residual in each bin. About 95% of the points should fall inside the ±2 standard error bands.

binned <- hmda %>%
  mutate(p_hat = fitted(logit_full),   # predicted probability for each applicant
         resid = deny01 - p_hat,       # raw residual: observed (0/1) minus predicted
         bin = ntile(p_hat, 20)) %>%   # 20 groups of equal size by predicted probability
  group_by(bin) %>%
  summarise(p_mean = mean(p_hat),      # average prediction in the bin
            resid_mean = mean(resid),  # average residual in the bin
            se2 = 2 * sqrt(p_mean * (1 - p_mean) / n())) # +/- 2 standard errors

ggplot(binned, aes(x = p_mean, y = resid_mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = -se2, ymax = se2), fill = "#e8e3d3") + # band where ~95% of points should fall
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40") +
  geom_point(color = "#4b2e83", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Mean Predicted Probability of Denial", y = "Mean Residual",
       title = "Binned Residual Plot (20 Bins)") +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation: if many points fall outside the band, or the points form a clear pattern, the model is missing something (a nonlinear term, an interaction or an omitted variable). Like before, a good looking plot does not prove zero conditional mean.

In our case: all 20 points sit inside the band, and they move above and below zero without a clear trend. Most bins have predicted probabilities below 0.2, because most applicants have a low chance of denial; the last bin (about 0.75) holds the high risk applicants. The band is narrow near 0 and wider in the middle, because the binomial variance P(1−P) is largest near 0.5. Two bins around 0.13 to 0.17 sit a little low (the model slightly overpredicts denial there), but they are still inside the band. Overall, the fit looks acceptable.

Adjustment to the Logistic Regression

Based on the checks, we make three changes:

  1. Remove the five applications with pirat >1. Payments larger than income are not realistic for a mortgage applicant.
  2. Add a squared term for pirat using I(), so the effect of debt can grow faster at high ratios.
  3. Group lvrat into categories: low (<0.8), medium (0.8 to 0.95) and high (0.95 or above). Lenders often use these cutoffs because a loan above 80% of the home value usually needs mortgage insurance.
hmda_clean <- hmda %>%
  filter(pirat <= 1) %>%              # drop the 5 applications with payments above income
  mutate(lvrat_cat = cut(lvrat,       # turn loan to value into three groups
                         breaks = c(-Inf, 0.8, 0.95, Inf),
                         labels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
                         right = FALSE)) # intervals like [0.8, 0.95): 0.8 goes to "medium"

# check how many applications (and denials) fall in each group
table(hmda_clean$lvrat_cat, hmda_clean$deny)
##         
##            no  yes
##   low    1305  104
##   medium  742  145
##   high     47   32

To compare models fairly with AIC or BIC, they must use the same data. So we refit the original model on hmda_clean first.

# update() refits an existing model; here only the data change
logit_clean <- update(logit_full, data = hmda_clean)

# adjusted model: squared pirat term + loan to value groups
# I() tells R to compute pirat^2 as a number before using it in the formula
logit_adj <- glm(deny ~ pirat + I(pirat^2) + hirat + lvrat_cat + chist +
                   mhist + phist + selfemp + insurance + afam,
                 data = hmda_clean, family = binomial)
summary(logit_adj)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = deny ~ pirat + I(pirat^2) + hirat + lvrat_cat + 
##     chist + mhist + phist + selfemp + insurance + afam, family = binomial, 
##     data = hmda_clean)
## 
## Coefficients:
##                 Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
## (Intercept)      -3.7232     0.6823  -5.457 4.85e-08 ***
## pirat            -4.1490     3.4835  -1.191 0.233637    
## I(pirat^2)       12.0879     4.2340   2.855 0.004305 ** 
## hirat            -0.6101     1.2803  -0.477 0.633712    
## lvrat_catmedium   0.4893     0.1639   2.985 0.002839 ** 
## lvrat_cathigh     1.5795     0.3105   5.087 3.64e-07 ***
## chist2            0.7661     0.2141   3.578 0.000346 ***
## chist3            0.9182     0.3180   2.888 0.003883 ** 
## chist4            1.5786     0.3318   4.758 1.96e-06 ***
## chist5            1.1932     0.2495   4.783 1.73e-06 ***
## chist6            1.5482     0.2352   6.582 4.64e-11 ***
## mhist2            0.3993     0.1956   2.042 0.041172 *  
## mhist3            0.5194     0.4755   1.092 0.274719    
## mhist4            0.2354     0.6553   0.359 0.719365    
## phistyes          1.2747     0.2105   6.056 1.40e-09 ***
## selfempyes        0.6444     0.2160   2.983 0.002856 ** 
## insuranceyes      4.5786     0.5608   8.165 3.21e-16 ***
## afamyes           0.6453     0.1806   3.574 0.000352 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)
## 
##     Null deviance: 1726.9  on 2374  degrees of freedom
## Residual deviance: 1247.4  on 2357  degrees of freedom
## AIC: 1283.4
## 
## Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 6

With a squared term, we cannot read pirat alone. The linear term is negative but not significant, and the squared term is positive and significant. Together they say: denial odds change little at low debt ratios and rise quickly at high ones. This matches the empirical logit plot.

Compare Logistic Models

Likelihood Ratio Test

For nested models (one model is the other plus extra terms), the likelihood ratio test checks whether the extra terms improve the fit. It compares the deviances. Here we test whether the squared term is needed.

# the same model without the squared term (". ~ . -" means keep everything, minus this)
logit_no_sq <- update(logit_adj, . ~ . - I(pirat^2))

# likelihood ratio test: does the bigger model fit significantly better?
anova(logit_no_sq, logit_adj, test = "Chisq")
## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model 1: deny ~ pirat + hirat + lvrat_cat + chist + mhist + phist + selfemp + 
##     insurance + afam
## Model 2: deny ~ pirat + I(pirat^2) + hirat + lvrat_cat + chist + mhist + 
##     phist + selfemp + insurance + afam
##   Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi)   
## 1      2358     1255.8                        
## 2      2357     1247.4  1   8.3815 0.003791 **
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The p value is about 0.004, so the squared term significantly improves the model.

Model Summary Table

modelsummary works with glm() too. Use exponentiate = TRUE to show odds ratios instead of log odds.

modelsummary(
  list(
    "Simple" = logit_simple,
    "Full (cleaned data)" = logit_clean,
    "Adjusted" = logit_adj
  ),
  exponentiate = TRUE, # show odds ratios instead of log odds
  stars = TRUE,        # significance stars
  fmt = 3,             # 3 decimal places
  title = "Logistic Regression of Mortgage Denial (Odds Ratios)",
  output = "html")

Performance Metrics

AIC and BIC [smaller - better]: same meaning as in the linear model.

Pseudo R-squared [larger - better]: there is no true R-squared for logistic regression. The most common substitute is McFadden’s pseudo R-squared, 1−log⁡Lmodellog⁡Lnull. Values between 0.2 and 0.4 are usually seen as a good fit. Do not compare it directly with an OLS R-squared.

# null model: intercept only, used as the baseline for pseudo R-squared
logit_null <- glm(deny ~ 1, data = hmda_clean, family = binomial)

# small helper function: McFadden pseudo R-squared = 1 - logLik(model) / logLik(null)
mcfadden <- function(model) {
  1 - as.numeric(logLik(model)) / as.numeric(logLik(logit_null))
}

# collect the fit measures of both models in one small table
data.frame(
  model = c("Full (cleaned data)", "Adjusted"),
  AIC = c(AIC(logit_clean), AIC(logit_adj)),
  BIC = c(BIC(logit_clean), BIC(logit_adj)),
  McFadden_R2 = c(mcfadden(logit_clean), mcfadden(logit_adj))
)
##                 model      AIC      BIC McFadden_R2
## 1 Full (cleaned data) 1300.755 1393.119   0.2652950
## 2            Adjusted 1283.400 1387.309   0.2776612

In our case: the adjusted model has lower AIC (1283 vs 1301), lower BIC (1387 vs 1393) and higher pseudo R-squared (0.278 vs 0.265). We will use it for prediction.

Look at afamyes across the three models in the table. The odds ratio drops from about 3.6 (simple) to about 1.9 (adjusted). Much of the raw gap is linked to differences in credit history and debt. But a significant gap remains after these controls. This is an association in observational data. It does not by itself prove discrimination, because other relevant factors may still be missing.

Prediction with Logistic Regression

predict() for a glm() model has two scales, set by type:

  • type = "link" (default): the predicted log odds.
  • type = "response": the predicted probability of Y=1.
predict(logit_adj, type = "link")[1]     # first applicant: predicted log odds
##         1 
## -2.102765
predict(logit_adj, type = "response")[1] # first applicant: predicted probability
##         1 
## 0.1088283
# plogis() converts log odds back to probability: exp(x) / (1 + exp(x))
plogis(predict(logit_adj, type = "link")[1])
##         1 
## 0.1088283

This is the same issue we had with the log price model. The default output (-2.10) is on the transformed scale. We need to transform it back, here with the logistic function instead of exp(). The first applicant has about an 11% predicted chance of denial.

From Probability to Classification

To turn probabilities into yes/no predictions, we pick a threshold. The default choice is 0.5.

# predicted probability of denial for every applicant
hmda_clean$p_hat <- predict(logit_adj, type = "response")

# classify: "yes" if the probability is above 0.5
hmda_clean$pred_05 <- ifelse(hmda_clean$p_hat > 0.5, "yes", "no")

# confusion matrix: rows = what the model says, columns = what really happened
table(predicted = hmda_clean$pred_05, actual = hmda_clean$deny)
##          actual
## predicted   no  yes
##       no  2066  188
##       yes   28   93

The overall accuracy is (2066+93)/2375≈91%. That sounds good, but a model that predicts “no” for everyone would already be about 88% accurate, because only 12% of applications are denied. Our model only catches 93 of the 281 denials (33%).

When the outcome is rare, a lower threshold is often more useful. Try the overall denial rate as the threshold:

# use the overall denial rate (about 0.12) as the threshold instead of 0.5
hmda_clean$pred_rate <- ifelse(hmda_clean$p_hat > mean(hmda_clean$deny01), "yes", "no")
table(predicted = hmda_clean$pred_rate, actual = hmda_clean$deny)
##          actual
## predicted   no  yes
##       no  1719   82
##       yes  375  199

Now we catch 199 of 281 denials (71%), but we also flag 375 approved applications by mistake. The right threshold depends on the cost of each type of error. We will look at this trade off (ROC curves, AUC) in Part B.

Average Marginal Effect: Back to Probabilities

Odds ratios are hard to explain to a general audience. An average marginal effect (AME) reports the change in probability instead. For a binary X like afam, we predict every applicant twice, once with afam = "yes" and once with afam = "no", keep everything else the same, and average the difference.

# two copies of the data: everyone set to afam = "yes", and everyone set to "no"
# (all other columns stay exactly as observed)
data_yes <- hmda_clean %>% mutate(afam = factor("yes", levels = c("no", "yes")))
data_no  <- hmda_clean %>% mutate(afam = factor("no",  levels = c("no", "yes")))

# predict both versions for every applicant, take the difference, then average it
mean(predict(logit_adj, newdata = data_yes, type = "response") -
     predict(logit_adj, newdata = data_no,  type = "response"))
## [1] 0.05486026

Holding all other variables at their observed values, being an African American applicant is associated with about a 5.5 percentage point higher probability of denial. Compare this with the odds ratio of about 1.9 for the same variable. Both are correct, but they answer different questions. (The marginaleffects package automates this for any model.)
