These questions ask you to read and interpret your own Part A output.

  1. [1 pt] In simple_lm, pick the coefficient on sqft. Write one sentence interpreting it in plain words, including its units (dollars per square foot) and whether it is statistically significant. How does its interpretation differ from the sqft coefficient in log_simple_lm?

    Hold year_built constant, every additional 1 sqft adds $501 value with p < 2e-16, means that is statistially significant. For the log_simple_lm one, the coefficient is the affct on log price, means that it shuold be interpreted as the exponentital function, which is the exponent of e. which roughly equallys 1.00036887, means that additional 1 sqft adds 0.037% of value.

  2. [1 pt] Look back at the Residuals vs Fitted and Q–Q plots for simple_lm. Which two OLS assumptions showed problems, and what did the log transformation of sale_price do to them? Assumption 5: residuals vs. fitted diagram is funnel shape, means that the higher the fitted value, more scattered the residual value becomes. Assumption 6: the points on the right side of the Q-Q plot curve is sharply upward, means that the residual value is higher when standardized residuals are higher. It may indicate that some properties are significantly undervalued by the model. After log, the residual values are more evenly spread, largest standaridized residuals decreased from 20 to about 6, but there remains a slight S-shape, indicating that the problem is not fully solved.

  3. [1 pt] We said a flat red line in Residuals vs Fitted does not prove zero conditional mean (E[ε∣X]=0). Name one variable that is almost certainly omitted from simple_lm and explain which direction it would bias the sqft coefficient. Location/View/Waterfront would be the omitted variable bias Better location has a positive effect on price, while houses in those location is oftenly larger, which also has a positive effect. The two positive effect makes the coefficient of sqft to be overestimated, as some premium of better location is wrongfully counted in size.

  4. [1 pt] Compare the “Without Interaction” and “Interaction” models in the modelsummary table. Using Adjusted R-squared and AIC/BIC, which model would you choose and why? Does the significant interaction term change how you interpret the sqft effect? Interaction model’s Adj.R square is higher, both AIC and BIC are lower, therefore I would choose it.The significant interaction does change how we interpret sqft. Without the intercration varaiable, the model gives all properties a rigid slope for sqft, when with it, the slope is about 0.00023 + 0,00004*condition. While 0.00023 represents the slope when condition is 0, which is probably not possible. The positive interaction means that condition adds value to the property when other varaiables are held constant.

  5. [1 pt] The VIF and Durbin–Watson results: report the values you got. Did either flag a concern? Given these are 2023 King County sales, why might the independence assumption still be violated even if Durbin–Watson looks acceptable? VIF: Both sqft and year_built are 1.096, far lower than 5, means that there is little multicollinerarity Durbin-Watson: 1.648, which is acceptable, means autocoorelation is okay. Even if DW is close to 2, the residuals may still show positive spatial autocorrealtion becasue nearby homes share neighbourhood characteristics.

  6. [1 pt] In the Prediction section, the first raw prediction from the log model was about 13.57, far below any real sale price. Explain why that happened and what exp() fixes. Then interpret: for the interaction model, why can’t we read exp(coef) on the sqft main effect as “the price change per sqft” the same way we did for log_simple_lm?

    Because the model’s outcome is log(slae_price), predict function returns a log price, not actual money, exp function converts it back to dollars. In log_simple_lm, exp(β) is a constant multiplier. In the interaction model, the sqft effect is 0.00023 + 0.00004 * condition, so the multiplier exp (0.00023 + 0.0004 * condition) depends on condition, exp (0.00023) alone applies only when condition = 0, which is virtually impossible.

Building and Checking a New Model

  1. [2 pts] Fit a new model called logit_ext that adds single, hschool and unemp to logit_adj. (Hint: `update(logit_adj, . ~ .
    • single + hschool + unemp)`.)
    • Run a likelihood ratio test comparing logit_adj and logit_ext. What are the null and alternative hypotheses? What do you conclude?
    • Report the AIC and BIC of both models. Do they agree? Explain why they might give different answers, and say which model you would keep.
    • Report the events per variable (EPV) for logit_ext. Is the sample still large enough?
logit_ext <- update(logit_adj, . ~ . + single + hschool + unemp)
stopifnot(identical(rownames(model.frame(logit_adj)),
                    rownames(model.frame(logit_ext))))
anova(logit_adj, logit_ext, test = "LRT")
## Analysis of Deviance Table
## 
## Model 1: deny ~ pirat + I(pirat^2) + hirat + lvrat_cat + chist + mhist + 
##     phist + selfemp + insurance + afam
## Model 2: deny ~ pirat + I(pirat^2) + hirat + lvrat_cat + chist + mhist + 
##     phist + selfemp + insurance + afam + single + hschool + unemp
##   Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi)   
## 1      2357     1247.4                        
## 2      2354     1234.2  3   13.181 0.004262 **
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
data.frame(model = c("Adjusted", "Extended"),
           AIC = AIC(logit_adj, logit_ext)$AIC,
           BIC = BIC(logit_adj, logit_ext)$BIC)
##      model      AIC      BIC
## 1 Adjusted 1283.400 1387.309
## 2 Extended 1276.219 1397.447
events <- sum(model.response(model.frame(logit_ext)) == "yes")
slopes <- logit_ext$rank - 1
c(events = events, slopes = slopes, EPV = events / slopes)
## events slopes    EPV 
## 281.00  20.00  14.05
   The likelihood ratio test rejects the null that all three added coefficients are zero, indicating that at least one different from 0. I would keep logit_ext because fit improves and AIC falls from 1283.4 to 1276.22. BIC penalizes complexity more heavily and rises from 1387.31 to 1397.45, favouring logit_adj. EPV is 14.05, > guideline of 10.

Prediction

  1. [2 pts] Use logit_adj to predict the probability of denial for the hypothetical applicant below, once with afam = "no" and once with afam = "yes".

    # helper: build a factor with the same levels as the column in hmda_clean
# (predict() needs new data to use exactly the same factor levels)
lv <- function(v, x) factor(x, levels = levels(hmda_clean[[v]]))

# one row per scenario: same applicant, afam = "no" (row 1) and "yes" (row 2)
applicant <- data.frame(
  pirat = 0.35, hirat = 0.28, lvrat_cat = lv("lvrat_cat", "medium"),
  chist = lv("chist", "2"), mhist = lv("mhist", "2"),
  phist = lv("phist", "no"), selfemp = lv("selfemp", "no"),
  insurance = lv("insurance", "no"), afam = lv("afam", c("no", "yes"))
)
    • Report the two predicted probabilities and their difference in percentage points.
    • Compute the ratio of their odds, and compare it with exp(coef(logit_adj)["afamyes"]). Why are the two numbers the same, while the ratio of the two probabilities is not?
lv <- function(v, x) factor(x, levels = levels(hmda_clean[[v]]))
applicant <- data.frame(
  pirat = 0.35, hirat = 0.28, lvrat_cat = lv("lvrat_cat", "medium"),
  chist = lv("chist", "2"), mhist = lv("mhist", "2"),
  phist = lv("phist", "no"), selfemp = lv("selfemp", "no"),
  insurance = lv("insurance", "no"), afam = lv("afam", c("no", "yes"))
)
p <- unname(predict(logit_adj, newdata = applicant, type = "response"))
odds <- p / (1 - p)
data.frame(afam = applicant$afam, probability = p, odds = odds)
##   afam probability      odds
## 1   no  0.09879652 0.1096273
## 2  yes  0.17287773 0.2090111
c(difference_percentage_points = 100 * diff(p),
  odds_ratio = odds[2] / odds[1],
  exp_coefficient = unname(exp(coef(logit_adj)["afamyes"])),
  probability_ratio = p[2] / p[1])
## difference_percentage_points                   odds_ratio 
##                     7.408121                     1.906560 
##              exp_coefficient            probability_ratio 
##                     1.906560                     1.749836

Changing afam from no to yes raises predicted denail probability from 9.88% to 17.29%. Since β_afam measures the change in log-odds, exponentiating gives the odds rator of 1.90656. Dividing the probability gives 1.749836.

  1. [1 pt] Build a confusion matrix for logit_adj with a threshold of 0.3. Report (a) the share of actual denials the model catches and
    1. the share of actual approvals it wrongly flags. Compared with the 0.5 threshold in the lab, what did you gain and what did you lose?
p_hat <- fitted(logit_adj)
for (threshold in c(0.3, 0.5)) {
  predicted <- factor(ifelse(p_hat > threshold, "yes", "no"),
                      levels = c("no", "yes"))
  cm <- table(predicted, actual = hmda_clean$deny)
  print(threshold)
  print(cm)
  print(c(denials_caught = cm["yes", "yes"] / sum(cm[, "yes"]),
          approvals_flagged = cm["yes", "no"] / sum(cm[, "no"])))
}
## [1] 0.3
##          actual
## predicted   no  yes
##       no  2010  147
##       yes   84  134
##    denials_caught approvals_flagged 
##        0.47686833        0.04011461 
## [1] 0.5
##          actual
## predicted   no  yes
##       no  2066  188
##       yes   28   93
##    denials_caught approvals_flagged 
##        0.33096085        0.01337154
At 0.3, the model catches 134 of the 281 actual denials, and wrongfuly flags 84 of the 2,094 approvals. At 0.5, it is 93 and 28. Lowering the threshold identifies 41 additional denials in the cost of 56 extra false alarms.

Linking the Linear and Logistic Models

  1. [1 pt] In both log_simple_lm and logit_adj we take exp() of a coefficient. Explain what exp(coef) means in each model (what is being multiplied?). Then explain why predict() returned 13.57 for the log price model and -2.10 for the logistic model, and which function brings each back to a meaningful scale.
exp(predict(log_interaction_lm, newdata = sales[1, ]))
##        1 
## 785876.9
eta <- unname(predict(logit_adj, type = "link")[1])
c(log_odds = eta, odds = exp(eta), probability = plogis(eta))
##    log_odds        odds probability 
##  -2.1027653   0.1221183   0.1088283
Holding other variables fixed, exp(β_sqft) multiplies fitted price /sqft. exp(β_afam) multiples denials odds when afam changes from no to yes. exp(13.57456) converts log price to $785.877 and plogis (-2.102765) converts log-odds to a 10.88* denical chance.
  1. [1 pt] The odds ratio for afamyes drops from about 3.6 in logit_simple to about 1.9 in logit_adj. Using the omitted variable reasoning from the linear TODO (Question 3), explain why it dropped. Name one variable that is not in the HMDA data but could still bias the afamyes estimate, and say why we should call the result an association rather than proof of discrimination.
logit_simple <- glm(deny ~ pirat + afam, data = HMDA, family = binomial())
# The middle column isolates the change in sample from the change in model.
simple_clean <- update(logit_simple, data = hmda_clean)
sapply(list(simple_original = logit_simple, simple_clean = simple_clean,
            adjusted_clean = logit_adj),
       function(model) unname(exp(coef(model)["afamyes"])))
## simple_original    simple_clean  adjusted_clean 
##        3.570772        3.536932        1.906560
The simple model contorls only for payment-to-income ratio. The afam odds ratio falls from 3.57 to 1.91 in the adjusted model, means that the differnce in credit history and loan characteristics is partially the explaner of the gap. Liquid savings remain unmeasured, this could be a estimation bias if savings differed across groups and influenced lending decisions. The remaining association alone cannot establish discrimination. The logistic regression estimates how denial odds differ across racial groups after accounting for the financial informaiton in he data, it cannot account for other human decision factors such as history and personal bias.

📖 Optional: Logistic Regression in a Research Paper (Not Graded)

Optional and not graded. This reading shows how the logistic regression from the lab is used in published housing research. It is good practice for your final project and for reading papers in other courses.

This section does not require any coding or submission.

In this section, we will read a recent research paper published by Runstad Department faculty Rebecca J. Walter, Arthur Acolin, Ruoniu (Vince) Wang, Gregg Colburn, along with people from other institutions: Exploring the association between household compositional change and mobility of subsidized householders in the United States. You are able to find the PDF version within the lab folder.

This study examines the relationship between household compositional change (such as a partner, child, or adult entering or leaving the household) and residential mobility of subsidized householders in the US. They use the Annual Longitudinal Files 2005–2018 from U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, which is restricted-use data required researchers to apply to access. Northwest Federal Statistical Research Data Center is the center within UW partnered with U.S. Census Bureau to provide such data access.

Please skim the paper first and use the following to guide your further reading, especially about the Data and methods and Results parts.

Settings

  1. What is the unit of analysis of this study? What is the sample size N? Is this study cross-sectional or longitudinal (lecture 2 data)?
  2. Why do you think U.S. Census Bureau requires us apply for the data usage instead of providing public access like American Community Survey (ACS) data?
  3. In a research paper, we tend to include two parts of explanatory variables: (1) the key explanatory variables (or variables of interest), which directly address the research question; and (2) the control variables, which account for other factors that might also influence the response variable. In this paper, what are the key explanatory variables and response variable?
  4. What is the purpose of including local market characteristics as part of X? Even though we do not have access to the data, which variables could be multicollinear with local market characteristics?
  5. Can we use normal linear regression for this study?
  6. The follow picture shows model specification in page 8 of this paper. Do you find any problem with this equation and explanation, especially for the explanatory variable part?

Model Configurations and Results

This study uses logistic regression, which we practiced with the HMDA data in the lab section above. We replace Y with log⁡(P/(1−P)), where P is the probability of Y=1. This post from IBM is also helpful. Think about this model:

log⁡(P1−P)=β0+β1X1+β2X2

  1. How should we interpret β1?
  2. In the result tables of this paper, they use Odds Ratio rather than the coefficient of X. How could you calculate the coefficient β for Household Member Enters or Exits (with odd ratio of 1.671)? The table below shows part of the results.
  3. How much more likely are households with a compositional change (a member entering or exiting) to move, compared to those without, controlling for other factors?
  4. What are the null and alternative hypotheses being tested by the t-value (398.7) for “Household Member Enters or Exits” in Model 1? What is the meaning of ‘***’?
  5. They conducted at least three logistic regression models. Why did they do that?
  6. The authors only use tables to present results. What is one way to visualize the adds ratio from this logistic model to show uncertainty of the results? You can use a plot example to illustrate.
  7. The title of this paper uses association rather than effect, impact, or influence. Authors are also very cautious term usages in main text. What is the reason?
